system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2129-12-22 08:00:00 to 2129-12-25 14:07:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with chronic pancreatitis, type 2 diabetes, and a history of Puestow procedure was admitted for severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Imaging revealed a partial small bowel obstruction without a clear transition point, along with a reducible ventral hernia. He was managed conservatively with NPO status, IV fluids, pain control, and manual hernia reduction. His psychiatric history, including depression and PTSD, was addressed with medication adjustments. By hospital day three, he tolerated a regular diet, remained pain-free, and was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up plans. No surgical intervention was required.
problems: Major depressive affective disorder, recurrent episode, severe, specified as with psychotic behavior
Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Ventral, unspecified, hernia without mention of obstruction or gangrene
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

The patient with ventral hernia s/p Puestow procedure was 
admitted to the General Surgical Service for elective hernia 
repair with mesh. On ___, the patient underwent ventral 
incisional hernia repair with mesh , which went well without 
complication (reader referred to the Operative Note for 
details). After a brief, uneventful stay in the PACU, the 
patient arrived on the floor NPO, on IV fluids and antibiotics, 
with a foley catheter and a JP drain in place, and Dilaudid PCA 
for pain control. The patient was hemodynamically stable.
.
Post-operative pain was initially well controlled with Dilaudid 
PCA, which was converted to oral pain medication when tolerating

kept to low wall suction, patient was discharged home with JP

up appointment. Patient will continue on oral Keflex after 
discharge until his follow up appointment with the surgeon. 
Patient was discharged home with services o POD #3 in stable 
condition.

with stable vital signs. The patient was tolerating a regular 
diet, ambulating, voiding without assistance, and pain was well 
controlled. The patient received discharge teaching and 
follow-up instructions with understanding verbalized and 
agreement with the discharge plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the surgical team. You're here today for your scheduled hernia repair, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been having a lot of pain near my old incision, and they said the hernia was starting to block things a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the imaging showed part of your colon was partially stuck in the hernia. We were able to reduce it, but because the defect is large, surgery is the best option to prevent it from happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will you be using mesh? I remember last time they did the Puestow, it was a big surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll be doing a primary repair with Prolene mesh overlay. It helps strengthen the area and reduces the chance of the hernia coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And how long will I be out after the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stay in the hospital for a few days. We’ll start you on IV fluids and pain medication, and gradually get you back on food once your bowels start working again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had gastroparesis before—will that be a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware of your history. We’ll start you on clear liquids on post-op day one and advance slowly. We’ll also continue your pancreatic enzymes and monitor how you tolerate things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my diabetes—should I take my metformin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll hold metformin while you’re not eating and switch to insulin if needed. We’ll restart it once you’re on a regular diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, makes sense. What about my other meds—like for my mood and nerves?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll resume most of your psychiatric medications as soon as you’re able to take pills. The team will coordinate with psychiatry to make sure nothing is missed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had some PTSD flare-ups lately—work stuff, old memories. I hope I can sleep okay here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can help with that. You’re on prazosin and zolpidem at home—we’ll restart those as appropriate. Let the nurses know if you’re having trouble resting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from surgery. The procedure went very well—ventral hernia repair with mesh, no complications. You’re in the recovery unit now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks… I feel groggy. Is the drain in my side normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we placed a JP drain in your right lower quadrant to collect any fluid and prevent buildup. It will stay in until your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s temporary. We’ll remove it tonight or tomorrow morning once you’re up and moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain’s okay right now. I see the PCA button—should I use it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, use it as needed. It’s hydromorphone, and it’s safe when used properly. We’ll switch to oral meds once you start eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs look stable. Glucose was 154 this morning—well controlled. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try some water or ice chips today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on clear liquids—water, broth, apple juice. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance your diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds—will I still get the PCA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it for now, but once you’re on oral pain meds, we’ll discontinue it. Chronic pain service reviewed your case and recommended continuing gabapentin and adding acetaminophen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on a lot of meds—can you tell me which ones I’ll restart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart most: lisinopril, simvastatin, omeprazole, amitriptyline, ziprasidone, duloxetine, gabapentin, metformin once you’re eating, and your pancreatic enzymes with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the stool softener? I don’t want to strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll give you docusate twice a day and senna at night to help. Avoid heavy lifting for at least six weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling? Any nausea or pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain is about a 3. I had some broth and jello—no nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll upgrade you to a soft diet tomorrow—maybe mashed potatoes, applesauce. And we removed the catheter this morning—you voided fine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no problem. The drain is a little annoying, but I’ll manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re tolerating food well. We’re advancing you to a regular diet. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About a 4, but manageable. I’m on oral meds now—hydromorphone as needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and acetaminophen regularly. We discontinued the PCA. You’re walking well—great job with the ambulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I get discharged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If all goes well today, we’re planning for tomorrow morning. You need to tolerate a regular diet, be pain-controlled, and have no fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be going home with the drain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’ll stay in until your follow-up. You’ll need to empty it daily, keep the site clean, and watch for signs of infection—increased redness, fever, or cloudy drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll take Keflex four times a day for 14 days to prevent infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve done well—afebrile, eating, walking, pain controlled. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my staples?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll be removed at your follow-up. You can shower—just pat the area dry. No baths or swimming until then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And activity?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No lifting over 10 pounds, no driving while on pain meds. Continue walking daily. Follow up with surgery and your PCP in one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I understand. I’ll take my meds, care for the drain, and call if anything’s wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re doing great. We’ll see you in clinic to remove the staples and drain. Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic pancreatitis, type 2 diabetes, gastroparesis, and prior Puestow procedure was admitted for elective repair of a symptomatic incisional hernia that had caused a minor bowel obstruction. He underwent an uncomplicated open ventral incisional hernia repair with Prolene mesh overlay on hospital day one. Postoperatively, he was managed with IV fluids, antibiotics, a JP drain, and pain control via PCA initially, transitioning to oral medications. His diet was advanced from clear liquids on postoperative day one to a regular diet by day three. He voided independently after catheter removal, remained afebrile, and had stable vital signs. He was discharged home on postoperative day three with instructions for incision and drain care, oral Keflex, and follow-up. His chronic conditions, including hypertension, bipolar disorder, PTSD, and diabetes, were managed with continuation of most home medications.
